Well, maybe the Minard method can induce/infer a stage for them

reply_text:
㊥ Gist: The Minard method does have a built-in guess for this, a stage prior for each library directory. But the guess is poor. When I scored it against the 689 hand labels, the directory prior matched only 36% of patterns, and a leave-one-out majority vote within each directory matched 35%. Always answering the most common stage would score 21%, so inferring from the directory gives a stage table that is about two-thirds wrong for those patterns. I'd have a Kimi seat read the 97 instead, which is how the original labels were made.

㊬ (what I measured just now)
- **Directory prior (`pattern-stage-dir-priors-2026-09-21.edn`):** matches the hand label on 248 of 684 patterns, 38% when weighted by hits.
- **Leave-one-out majority of labelled siblings:** 237 of 670 (35%).
- **Coverage of the 97:** 90 have labelled siblings, 5 have only a prior, and 2 have neither.

Directories mix stages heavily. For example, `test-registry` contains assurance patterns and select patterns side by side, so a pattern's location says little about its stage.

🈖 (labelling is already a model reading) The 689 existing labels weren't made by hand: agents read each pattern's source text and quoted the line that justified the choice. They are still "provisional pending Joe's blind check". So reading the 97 the same way isn't extra rigour, it's simply the method. A Kimi pack of ten patterns, each with its IF/THEN text inlined, takes about 5 minutes. Ten packs on the five Kimi seats would take under half an hour.

㊫ (an inference that might work) The patterns already have embeddings in futon3a, so each new pattern could take the stage of its nearest labelled neighbours. I haven't tested it. It is worth using only if a leave-one-out score on the 689 comes out well above the directory's 35%, which is a quick check if you'd prefer inference to reading.

🈸 (one decision) Shall I have the Kimi seats read the 97 patterns, in ten packs? Reply `yes` to proceed, or `embed` to run the nearest-neighbour check first.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: Gist: The Minard method doesn't label your turns directly. Each turn takes its stage from the pattern the search ranked first for it, so every library pattern needs a stage written down once, by reading the pattern. That is "labelling patterns". 97 patterns retrieved since 21 September have never been given a stage, so 153 of the 1,255 matched turns can't be counted.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (what one label is) This is a real entry from `pattern-stages-2026-09-21.edn`:

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (what's needed now) The 97 unlabelled patterns are mostly recent library additions. The top ones are `test-registry/bind-the-subject` (13 hits), `translation/test-by-reproducing-behaviour` (9) and `math-strategy/proof-architecture` (6). They are listed with hit counts in `pattern-stage-unlabelled-2026-10-01.json`. Labelling them is about ten Kimi jobs of ten patterns each, after which the stage table and figure can be rebuilt for 22 August to today.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (whether to bother) We could skip it and report those 153 hits (12%) as unlabelled. They aren't a random 12%, though: they cluster in the newest work, test-registry and translation in particular. Leaving them out would undercount whatever stages those patterns belong to, and that skew falls on the last ten days. Last turn's comparison also matters here. Minard's stage tells you about the topics your turns raised, not what each turn did. If you want the figure for that reason, labelling is worth doing. If you mainly wanted it to check 象, the near-chance result already says it can't serve that purpose.
